title: Piron, Handy and Oliver records compared to New Orleans bands
summary: How eastern bands sound legitimate on record, Peter Bocage's view of Louis, and the Oliver records surprising New Orleans.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Trumpeters I admired: rating the horn players

blocks.x: probably plenty of old rough players but they weren't probably the best and they probably didn't know too many tunes. But to play a large number of rags you probably had to be didn't have to be but most of them were. So I think as I say the only thing we can judge from now since we weren't around in the 1900s early 1900s to hear the music down here or any place else. one thing we have to go by are the records and if you listen to the eastern bands the things that they recorded compared to the New Orleans bands in particular they sound awfully legitimate most of them. Even things like the Handy Orchestra which was probably all written out. Maybe a few good numbers and a few blues but they don't they certainly don't swing and they don't have any freshness or much originality of the playing certainly that you can tell from the records. On the other hand there's the Pirone band which probably read a lot of things too and had arrangements made. Some of their things may be a little cut and dried and legitimate sounding too but at times they did sound pretty good and quite fresh sound to it. But it isn't one of my favorite hardly a typical rough style New Orleans band like Peter Boccage for instance.
